title: Summer Pudding
subtitle: Moulded pudding of summer berries in white bread
excerpt: A pudding basin lined with white bread and packed with stewed summer berries, weighted overnight until the bread is completely saturated and the berries set. Turned out and served with cream.

recipe.sourceNotes: Summer pudding was first recorded in British cookery books in the late 19th century, originally served to invalids and the elderly as a lighter alternative to the suet puddings that dominated winter menus. The name first appeared in print in 1904. It is one of the few truly cold British desserts, requiring no cooking beyond briefly stewing the fruit. The genius of the dish is the way the bread, initially a utilitarian container, transforms into something silky and deeply flavoured as it absorbs the fruit juices. Use very fresh, slightly stale white bread, not a crusty loaf.

content.text: The bread must be very fresh but not crusty: a medium-sliced white sandwich loaf is ideal. Cut the crusts off and overlap the slices to line the basin with no gaps, as the pudding will fall apart when turned out if there are holes in the bread. Weight the pudding with something heavy: a tin of beans on a plate directly on the pudding surface. The longer it chills (ideally overnight), the better it will be.

Put all the fruit except the strawberries and raspberries in a pan with the sugar and 2 tablespoons of water. Simmer for 3 to 4 minutes until the blackcurrants and redcurrants release their juice. Remove from the heat and stir in the strawberries and raspberries. Leave to cool slightly.

Line a 1.2-litre pudding basin with cling film, leaving enough overhanging to cover the top. Line with bread slices, cutting to fit and overlapping tightly with no gaps. Reserve enough bread for the top.

Spoon the fruit and most of its juice into the basin. Reserve a few tablespoons of juice. Cover the top with the remaining bread. Fold the cling film over. Set a small plate directly on top and weight it down. Refrigerate overnight.
To serve, unwrap and turn out onto a serving plate. Pour the reserved juice over any pale patches of bread. Serve in slices with cold double cream.
